extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science, constitutional law, and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: A close, normative analysis of the structural qualities, risks, and practical effects that distinguish the American (federal/national) Constitution from other federal/confederate systems; aimed at assessing what features make a federal constitution effective or dangerous. Emphasizes judiciary, legislature, executive, enforcement capacity, and the balance between local freedom and national strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: High rank and prerogatives of the Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: “The supreme court is the sole tribunal of the nation. Its power extends to all the cases arising under laws and treaties made by the executive and legislative authorities, to all cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction, and in general to all points which affect the law of nations. … its prerogatives are almost entirely political.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains scope: national questions, treaties, admiralty, inter-state suits; emphasizes that the Court sits above ordinary tribunals and that its decisions have major political consequences for the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges must be statesmen: information, integrity, and political awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The federal judges must not only be good citizens, and men possessed of that information and integrity which are indispensable to magistrates, but they must be Statesmen — politicians, not unread in the signs of the times…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides selection/evaluation of judges toward candidates with legal competence plus political judgment, courage to resist encroachments, and sensitivity to threats against union supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-stakes competence and prudence of the Court's composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If the supreme court is composed of imprudent men or bad citizens, “the Union may be plunged into anarchy or civil war.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions the prudence and character of the seven federal judges as fundamental to national tranquility and even existence — a central evaluative criterion when judging judicial appointments or institutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence (protected compensation and tenure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal constitution provides for the independence of the judges “by declaring that their salary shall not be altered, and that their functions shall be inalienable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains institutional safeguards for judicial independence (salary protection, inalienable functions). Note appended nuance: actual constitutional phrasing prevents diminution of compensation during continuance in office (not absolute immunity from any alteration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of public opinion as a limit and source of judicial legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Their power is enormous, but it is clothed in the authority of public opinion. They are the all-powerful guardians of a people which respects law; but they would be impotent against popular neglect or popular contempt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies judges must maintain legitimacy with the public; judicial power depends on public esteem and cannot safely exceed or fall short of public expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative independence through term-length and bicameral design
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures’ short terms make them narrowly dependent on constituents; the federal constitution increased term lengths and changed conditions/modes of election so representatives have “freer scope for the exercise of their own judgment,” and the Senate requires mature age and an indirectly elected body to secure superior intelligence and discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates legislative design by how insulated representatives are from short-term electoral pressures (longer terms, different modes of election, eligibility requirements, bicameral distinction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of concentration of powers and excessive legislative submissiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Two dangers to democracies: (1) the complete subjection of the legislative body to the caprices of the electoral body; and (2) the concentration of all the powers of the government in the legislative authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful constitution must provide institutional checks (separate executive, independent judiciary, differing legislative composition and terms) to avoid these twin evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive strength and independence within prescribed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal executive powers vested in a single individual with a four-year term; salary cannot be altered during the term; the president is protected by official dependents and armed with a suspensive veto to confer a strong and independent position within set limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates executive design by its capacity for independent action and protection from legislative manipulation while constrained by constitutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers and insulation of the judiciary from legislative influence
rubrics_metrics.description: In state constitutions the legislature often regulates judges’ emoluments or temporarily appoints judges, subjecting them to legislative influence; the federal constitution “carefully separates the judicial authority from all external influences.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures constitutional quality by the degree to which judicial functions, tenure, and compensation are insulated from legislative control or fusion of powers (no legislative bodies acting as superior courts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government must possess means of enforcement (direct effect on individuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike earlier confederations that demanded supplies from states, the American Union’s government “rules individuals… levies a tax… is served by its own civil and military officers, by its own army, and its own courts of justice” and can execute its own enactments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitution is effective only if the central government has direct authority and instruments (taxation, forces, courts) to enforce its laws — otherwise nominal powers become elements of discord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and wisdom of the framers/legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief cause of the federal constitution’s superiority lay in “the character of the legislators who composed it”; men chosen for intelligence and patriotism who proposed restrictions to guard liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard: the prudence, patriotism, and political knowledge of those who draft/implement a constitution materially affect its design and practical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing advantages of small and large political units
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of the federal system is “to unite the twofold advantages resulting from a small and from a large Territory” — preserving happiness and freedom of small communities while gaining the strength and civilizational benefits of great nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses federal arrangements by how well they allow local law to adapt to population exigencies and maintain civic vitality locally while enabling national strength and activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: strengthening powers requires independence but raises abuse risks
rubrics_metrics.description: “The more a power requires to be strengthened, the more extensive and independent it must be made; and the dangers which its abuse may create are heightened by its independence and its strength.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design must recognize the inherent trade-off: empowering central organs to perform functions requires insulating them, which increases the risk of abuse — the design must contain balancing safeguards.
